title: Hopscotch around the world: one court, many names

body.heading: The court and the marker
paragraphs: Draw a court of numbered squares — singles and pairs, usually eight to ten of them — ending in a safe “home”. Toss your marker into square one, then hop the court skipping the marked square: one foot in single squares, two feet in the pairs, turn at the top, and collect your marker on the way back.
A marker that lands on a line, a foot that touches a line, a hop into the marked square — any of these ends your turn. It is a game of balance, aim and honesty, playable by one player or ten.

body.heading: A court drawn on every continent
paragraphs: Hopscotch is found all over the world under local names and local court designs: Marelle in France, Rayuela in Spanish-speaking countries, courts scratched in schoolyards from India to Brazil. Some courts spiral; some add a “heaven” at the top that you must reach without a single fault.

Tradition claims very old roots for the game — courts resembling hopscotch have been linked to Roman times — but its true history is the schoolyard itself: a game so well designed that no generation has managed to improve it out of existence.

body.heading: Try it: design your own court
paragraphs: Chalk a classic court and play a full championship: each player must complete the court with the marker in every square, one fault and your turn passes. Then design a house court — add a spiral, a jump-across gap, a square where you must turn around twice.
Photograph your design before the rain takes it, and keep a court album. Chalk is temporary; that is the point. Every playground artist signs their work knowing the weather will clear the gallery.

takeaway: Hopscotch is a world language spoken in chalk: draw the court anywhere on Earth and somebody nearby knows how to play.
